title: Can Technology-Based Social Memory Aids Improve Social Engagement? Perceptions of a Novel Memory Aid for Persons With Memory Concerns.
authors: Horn BL, Albers EA, Mitchell LL, Jutkowitz E, Finlay JM, Millenbah AN, et al.
venue: Journal of applied gerontology : the official journal of the Southern Gerontological Society
finding_for_nametags: Twenty care dyads shown a wearable social memory aid expected it to reduce socializing-related stress for both the person with memory concerns and the family caregiver, but said that requiring visitors to have the app could limit its usefulness. Nametags identifies people by face and voice, so visitors need no app, but it has the analogous limit that it can name only the people a family member has enrolled.
method_and_sample: qualitative semi-structured interviews over Zoom (June–August 2020) after the aid was presented, 20 dyads of persons with memory concerns and family caregivers, thematic analysis; country not stated in the abstract
limitation: Participants were shown the aid rather than using it, so the reduced stress is anticipated, not measured, and they are described as persons with memory concerns, not specifically people with dementia.
supporting_sentence: However, certain features of the memory aid (e.g., visitors must have the app), could limit utility, and participants provided recommendations to enhance the tool.
note: Abstract only: the open-access full-text service returned HTTP 500 for PMC9957785 on two tries, and the record lists it as not open access. The abstract does not say how the aid identifies visitors or what it shows the wearer. Closest prior art in this batch: a wearable social memory aid aimed at the same problem (social engagement with memory loss).

title: Misidentification in patients with dementia.
authors: Nagaratnam N, Irving J, Kalouche H
finding_for_nametags: In a retrospective study of 116 dementia patients, 35% had some form of misidentification (of people, the 'phantom boarder', the mirror image or the 'TV sign'), and it was closely related to accusatory behavior. Misidentification is therefore common enough that truthful announcements and Nova answers can be expected to contradict what some wearers believe (tension 1), though the study does not look at correcting it.
method_and_sample: retrospective study, 116 dementia patients; setting and country not stated in the abstract
limitation: The abstract reports one 35% figure pooled across four different misidentification types, not the rate for misidentifying people alone, and the link to accusatory behavior was confounded by age, sex, cognitive impairment, stage and functional disability.
supporting_sentence: 35% had misidentification and there was a close relationship between misidentification and accusatory behavior.
note: Abstract only (no PMC copy). Inference, not tested: product.md says the wearer's face is not enrolled because the glasses never see it, but a mirror would show it, so the wearer's own reflection could get 'I don't recognize this person' (or match a look-alike relative); mirror-image misidentification is one of the four types counted here.

title: Famous faces and voices: Differential profiles in early right and left semantic dementia and in Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Luzzi S, Baldinelli S, Ranaldi V, Fabi K, Cafazzo V, Fringuelli F, et al.
finding_for_nametags: With perceptual deficits screened out, patients with early Alzheimer's disease were impaired at naming famous faces and voices but still recognized them, while semantic dementia patients were impaired at both naming and recognition. That fits the announcement's premise (give the name to someone who still knows the person) for early AD better than for semantic dementia, though the stimuli were famous people, not family.
method_and_sample: comparative neuropsychological study with a famous face and voice recognition and naming battery: 13 early semantic dementia patients (8 right-, 5 left-predominant temporal atrophy) and 25 AD patients, all without perceptual deficits; FDG-PET correlation in 12 SD; country not stated in the abstract
limitation: Small early-stage groups were tested on famous rather than personally familiar faces and voices, so the result may not carry over to recognizing family members or to later dementia.
supporting_sentence: Results showed a differential performance profile in the two diseases, because AD patients were significantly impaired in the naming tests, but showed preserved recognition, whereas SD patients were profoundly impaired both in naming and in recognition of famous faces and voices.
note: Abstract only (no PMC copy). It concerns patients' own recognition of people, not machine face or voice recognition. The abstract's sample line reads '25 CE patients'; from the rest of the abstract this appears to be the AD group. Naming failed for voices as well as faces in AD, so a name given on a voice match (voice-first presence) would address the same gap; that is an inference, not tested here.

title: Recognition of personally familiar faces and functional connectivity in Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Kurth S, Moyse E, Bahri MA, Salmon E, Bastin C
venue: Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
finding_for_nametags: Recognition of one's own and personally familiar faces from photographs was preserved in mild Alzheimer's disease but affected in moderate AD, which suggests the announcement and 'Who is this?' matter most for wearers past the mild stage. The study tested no aid.
method_and_sample: two behavioral experiments (mild AD, then moderate AD, each against healthy older adults) using photographs of self and familiar faces from different decades of life, with resting-state fMRI in the moderate group; sample sizes not given in the abstract
limitation: The abstract gives no sample sizes, and recognition was tested on photographs in a lab task rather than on live visitors.
supporting_sentence: However, in moderate AD, both self and familiar face recognition were affected.
note: Abstract only (no PMC copy). It concerns patients' own face recognition, not the system's. In mild AD, recent photographs were recognized faster than remote ones; background case reports cited in the abstract describe the reverse for self-faces in late-stage AD. Not a test of appearance change or long separation.

title: Informal carers' experience of assistive technology use in dementia care at home: a systematic review.
authors: Sriram V, Jenkinson C, Peters M
finding_for_nametags: In most of the 56 publications reviewed, carers' continuing engagement was key to whether assistive technology got used, and the authors found installation was often wrongly treated as a one-off event rather than an ongoing process. Nametags relies on a family member enrolling every person (photos, voice sample, facts), so it is likely to need re-enrollment as faces, voices and visitors change (tension 4), not a single setup.
method_and_sample: systematic review with narrative synthesis: 56 publications (50 studies; 30 qualitative, 17 quantitative, 9 mixed methods) from 19 countries, 2000–2018, reporting on 2016 carers of people with dementia living at home
limitation: It covers carers at home only (care homes and paid carers were excluded) and English-language studies, and its outcome measures were too varied to pool, so its conclusions are descriptive.
supporting_sentence: It is also clear from this review that installation of AT at home for use by someone who has dementia was often wrongly seen as a one-off event, rather than an ongoing process for getting the best out of AT.
note: Full text read; metadata from the Europe PMC record. None of the device types in its Table 2 is described as recognizing or naming people; the nearest are picture-button and photo-memory telephones. Quantitative studies rated devices useful but found no significant change in carer burden or well-being, and the authors note a lack of adverse-event reporting, so it gives no evidence on harm from a wrong name. Carers agreed people with dementia should be involved as much as possible in choosing and using technology, which bears on enrollment being run by a family member. It names repetitive questions among the symptoms hardest on carers; one included study's talking watch cut carers' questions about the time, a possible parallel for Nova and 'Who is this?' (inference).
